reading: Lund University's botanical garden is both a freely accessible city garden and a living collection used for teaching, research and conservation. Its eight hectares hold plants from around the world, arranged outdoors and in nine greenhouse climates; its greenhouse renovation makes a working garden temporarily rearrange itself around barriers. It cares about biodiversity, threatened local species, responsible growing, regional seed, and the relationships between plants and human life. Its vocabulary moves between families, origins, adaptations, collections and conservation on one hand, and guided walks, school lessons, seasons, fika and friends on the other. Distinctive tensions make this place more than a generic garden: desert and rainforest sit next door, a plant's label carries several languages and a family history, local meadow seeds support pollinators beyond the gates, and the garden is simultaneously a centuries-old university resource, an outdoor classroom and a neighborhood refuge.

enemies.idea: Climate seamstresses stitch desert heat to rainforest humidity, then drag the seam across a path so visitors must cross both extremes in a few steps.
enemies.why: The nine adjacent greenhouse climates become a moving terrain puzzle with visible seams to cut.

enemies.idea: A taxonomist with a rotating label-printer assigns each passerby a plant family and origin, then sends mechanical relatives to graft them into the matching bed.
enemies.why: Names, family and provenance become a dangerous classification game that can be fooled by swapping labels.

enemies.idea: The moth camera has learned to flag anything unfamiliar as invasive; its flash marks a target and summons tiny net-carrying interceptors.
enemies.why: A research identification system mistakes novelty for danger, making light and line of sight matter.

enemies.idea: A regional seed counter checks every seed against its supposed place of origin and fires unrecognized seeds away like hard little pellets.
enemies.why: A conservation problem becomes a precision projectile fight with a sorting mechanism to disrupt.

enemies.idea: The comfort warden trails retractable leashes and corrals any moving group into a perfectly orderly walking formation.
enemies.why: A recognizable garden rule becomes a choreography problem: break formation to stop the machine.

enemies.idea: A prehistoric-plant guide unfolds successive mechanical roots and fronds as it 'explains' the route, blocking each escape behind its audience.
enemies.why: The self-paced tour turns into an escalating living exhibit whose growth can be anticipated.

enemies.idea: A renovation scaffold walks on spindly jacks, fencing off each area it finishes and declaring the next bed under repair.
enemies.why: Construction barriers become a steadily expanding territorial threat with movable supports.

enemies.idea: A cold-house regulator swings violently between the Agathis house's warm and cool limits, dropping condensation and brittling metal on alternating cycles.
enemies.why: Its temperature rhythm telegraphs openings and changes how equipment behaves.

enemies.idea: A twelve-faced seasonal pruner strips whatever is currently flowering so that its own month can be the only season on display.
enemies.why: Each face attacks differently, from fruit flails to screens of scented leaves.

enemies.idea: A root-and-shoot lesson engine reenacts the journey from water to land, first flooding a path and then anchoring itself with cable roots.
enemies.why: The crew can interrupt an evolutionary sequence at different stages for different results.

enemies.idea: A spice mill sniffs out the warmest bodies and grinds aromatic clouds around them, masking the approach of smaller swarm machines.
enemies.why: A sensory lesson becomes a playful scent-and-visibility encounter.

enemies.idea: A soil-to-table harvester seizes any unattended object, plants it in a furrow and waits for a matching machine to sprout.
enemies.why: Its literal misunderstanding of cultivation gives the crew a chance to plant a decoy.

enemies.idea: An invasive-plant containment machine keeps extending its boundary around the next specimen until the protected collection and its visitors are trapped together.
enemies.why: Containment is the threat; opening a safe corridor requires redirecting its boundaries.

enemies.idea: A peat substitute tester sucks up soil in search of the perfect growing medium and spits sorted mounds that bury pathways and seedlings alike.
enemies.why: Its sorting process produces shifting cover and a clear way to jam it with the wrong material.

enemies.idea: A living-classroom examiner demands that everyone identify plants with all their senses; a wrong answer releases a probing mechanical tendril.
enemies.why: Observation and cooperation can defuse a confrontation without a straight fight.

enemies.idea: A group-tour marshal separates travelers into school, workplace and senior parties, then marches the separated groups along conflicting routes.
enemies.why: Its helpful group categories split a crew into a coordination challenge.

enemies.idea: A meadow surveyor measures every patch in square metres and rolls metal edging around anything it decides exceeds its allotted area.
enemies.why: A simple measurement becomes a tightening trap that can be tricked with a broken outline.

enemies.idea: A specimen-learning machine keeps removing parts from the nearest object so it can teach itself how that object works.
enemies.why: Object-based learning becomes a dismantling threat that can be distracted with expendable curiosities.

enemies.idea: An old coal-house stoker patrols with a boiler belly, mistaking any heap of dark material for fuel and sending soot through nearby glasshouses.
enemies.why: The café building's former fuel store supplies a memorable machine with an appetite to exploit.

enemies.idea: A survival-strategy mimic rapidly changes its armor after each environmental shock, borrowing the persistence of ancient plant groups.
enemies.why: Repeated tactics make it tougher, rewarding experimentation and restraint.

allies.idea: A pocket of meadow pollinators still visits real flowers and leads travelers along a chain of surviving seed patches beyond the swarm's fences.
allies.why: A distributed meadow network gives the crew a gentle, living route through occupied ground.

allies.idea: The local seed keepers maintain separate caches of wild-origin seed and trade a packet for help moving another cache to safety.
allies.why: Their small, portable mission connects conservation to practical choices about what to carry.

allies.idea: A garden educator uses touch, scent and patient questions to teach visitors how to tell a living plant from its machine imitation.
allies.why: The lesson gives the crew an actionable way to spot traps and protect specimens.

allies.idea: The garden's friends organize a quiet relay to water isolated beds, passing tools hand to hand under the patrols' notice.
allies.why: A community association becomes a network of guides and small acts of resistance.

allies.idea: Keepers of threatened Scanian plants share cuttings between hidden beds so no single raid can erase the collection.
allies.why: Their distributed refuge provides a tangible rescue objective and several possible safe havens.

bosses.idea: The Curator of Everything is a sprawling machine collection that catalogues each living thing by name, family and origin, then seals it into a climate-controlled compartment; it plans to preserve the whole garden by allowing nothing to interact.
bosses.why: It combines the garden's collections, labels and greenhouse climates into a fight about reopening connections between compartments.

bosses.idea: The Perpetual Renovator rebuilds the nine climate houses around itself, recycling barriers, scaffolds and climate controls into an ever-changing fortress that can never declare the work complete.
bosses.why: The garden-wide renovation becomes a mobile arena whose construction phases expose different weak points.

bosses.idea: The Head Gardener of One Perfect Bed turns lessons, seed production and conservation into a single enforced monoculture, uprooting anything that does not match its model specimen.
bosses.why: It twists the garden's whole mission of learning from diversity into a single escalating conflict over variety.

events.idea: A ceremony party has reached the southern garden, but a roaming construction barrier keeps moving the chosen gathering place. Help them make a temporary clear circle.
events.why: A peaceful occasion creates a precise, noncombat goal amid the renovation.

events.idea: A crate of regional seed has spilled into an ordinary seed pile. A keeper needs help sorting it before the machine counter arrives.
events.why: A tactile sorting task creates tension without making the seeds interchangeable treasure.

events.idea: An audio tour insists the next prehistoric specimen is behind a newly erected fence; the living specimen is actually visible from another side.
events.why: Observant crews can reconcile a fixed route with a changed garden.

events.idea: A moth camera flashes at a fluttering scrap caught in a branch, drawing interceptors toward a real moth resting just beneath it.
events.why: A quick choice of distraction or careful rescue turns a misidentification into a scene.

events.idea: A school-garden harvest is ready, but the mechanical harvester has planted its own metal imitation among the vegetables.
events.why: The crew can inspect and harvest carefully to feed allies while avoiding a surprise.

events.idea: A fragrant pile of ground spices has drifted across a path; follow the smell and find a stalled mill whose gears have caught on a baking stick.
events.why: A sensory clue leads to a machine that can be repaired, diverted or quietly bypassed.

events.idea: A label has been placed beside the wrong plant, and an inspection drone is about to remove the supposedly misplaced specimen.
events.why: Correcting a tiny piece of collection data can save a whole plant.

events.idea: Two neighboring greenhouse zones are leaking into one another; a wilted plant needs shade while a soaked mechanism blocks the dry route.
events.why: Contrasting climates make a small rescue into a route and resource puzzle.

events.idea: A meadow patch is about to be edged off by a surveyor. A pollinator is still traveling between it and another patch across the path.
events.why: The crew can preserve a visible ecological connection by moving the boundary.

events.idea: A temporary café cart is stranded on the wrong side of a cordon with a hot drink for the people tending a nearby bed.
events.why: A modest delivery creates an excuse to navigate the altered southern garden.

events.idea: A cold-house regulator is stuck at one end of its cycle; condensation reveals the shorted joint just before its next temperature swing.
events.why: The environment supplies both a timed hazard and the clue to fixing it.

events.idea: A gardener has three unlabeled soil mixtures and needs to choose one for a rescued plant while a peat-hungry sorter approaches.
events.why: A practical growing decision doubles as a chance to bait the machine.

events.idea: A group-tour marshal is leading two sets of visitors in opposite directions around the same bed; they need a signal to pass safely.
events.why: A simple traffic problem invites a clever signal or negotiation.

events.idea: The month's flowers have been clipped, but fruit and scented leaves still reveal which bed is thriving. A keeper asks the crew to find it.
events.why: Seasonal observation rewards attention beyond the obvious blossoms.

events.idea: A threatened local plant has one surviving cutting and two safe beds, each watched by a different patrol. Carry it to either refuge.
events.why: A fragile cargo and a meaningful route choice make a compact rescue.
